summary: This informational RFC gives guidelines and a template for writing extensions to the Incident Object Description Exchange Format (IODEF), which is defined in RFC 5070 and used to exchange incident management data.

eli5.summary: If you want to add a new box to a standard form, this tells you how to do it neatly.

questions: how to write an iodef extension
what is the iodef extension template
what is the iodef extension mechanism
subtitle: Template and guidelines for standardizing IODEF extensions

tldr.problem: IODEF (RFC 5070) defines a standard format for exchanging incident reports, but as new threat types emerge, organizations need to extend it with new fields. Without guidelines, extensions are inconsistent and hard to standardize.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC provides three extension mechanisms built into IODEF—extending enumerated attributes, adding structured data via AdditionalData elements, or wrapping IODEF in an external XML container—plus a template Internet-Draft authors can follow to document extensions clearly and consistently.
tldr.outcome: Organizations proposing IODEF extensions can now use a standard template and follow proven patterns, making the IETF review process faster and extensions more interoperable.

today: RFC 6684 is an Informational document and reference guide for IODEF extension authors. It has not been obsoleted. The template and mechanisms remain the standard way to propose IODEF extensions to the IETF.

sections.title: Why IODEF Needs Extensions
sections.content:
IODEF (Incident Object Description Exchange Format), defined in RFC 5070, is a standard XML format for describing and exchanging incident management data—incident reports, observations, impact information, and actions taken. Since IODEF's publication, the threat landscape has evolved and cooperative defense practices have improved, revealing the need for new types of data in incident reports.

This document is not a policy or governance document. Instead, it is a practical guide for engineers who wish to propose IODEF extensions. It describes when extension is appropriate, which of IODEF's three extension mechanisms to use, and provides a template for the Internet-Draft that documents the extension.

At the time of publication, the Managed Incident Lightweight Exchange (MILE) working group of the IETF provides a home for IODEF extension work.
sections.eli5: IODEF is the standard way to report security incidents. New threats came along that the old form didn't have boxes for. This document tells you how to add new boxes the right way.

sections.title: When to Extend IODEF
sections.content:
Before proposing an IODEF extension, ask two questions. First: does the problem actually involve reporting or sharing observations about an incident—a security event or group of events? If the answer is 'no', IODEF is probably not the right foundation. Second: can IODEF already represent the information without extension? IODEF has a rich set of incident classes and data types. If detailed examination of IODEF and consultation with experts shows the answer is 'yes', then extension is not necessary.

Examples of appropriate extensions include the following: leveraging external standards to make IODEF more expressive by referencing external incident databases; describing new types of entities involved (such as new actor roles); representing new types of indicators or observables; adding semantic metadata for handling or compliance purposes (such as data protection labeling).

This step prevents unnecessary extensions and keeps the core IODEF format stable.
sections.eli5: Before adding a new box to the form, check: is this about incidents? Can the form already say it? If both answers are yes, don't extend.

sections.title: Three Extension Mechanisms
sections.content:
IODEF was designed with three built-in ways to extend it. Choose based on what you are adding.

Mechanism 1: Extend Enumerated Attributes. Many IODEF elements have attributes with fixed lists of allowed values. For example, the Incident element's purpose attribute can be reporting, detection, or a few other values. To add a new value, set the attribute to ext-value and add a parallel ext-ATTR field with your custom value. This is the simplest way to add a few new options to an existing field.

Mechanism 2: Add Structured Data with AdditionalData or RecordItem. When you need to add entirely new fields or complex structures, use the AdditionalData or RecordItem elements. These can hold scalar data (numbers, strings, URIs) or XML. When using XML, define a schema for your extension, register the namespace and schema with IANA, and document it in your Internet-Draft.

Mechanism 3: Wrap IODEF in an External XML Container. For deep integration with external systems, you can contain an IODEF Document inside a larger XML document. This is less interoperable—pure IODEF tools will not understand the outer wrapper—but it allows full integration with external schemas. RID (RFC 6545) is an example.
sections.eli5: Three ways to add new stuff: add a new option to an existing field, stick new fields in an 'extra data' section, or wrap the whole form in a bigger form.

sections.title: The Extension Template
sections.content:
This RFC provides a template (in Appendix A) for Internet-Drafts that document IODEF extensions. The template covers the following sections:

  • Introduction: explain the problem the extension solves.
  • Terminology: define any new terms; reference IODEF and RFC 2119 keywords as needed.
  • Applicability: describe the use cases, scope, and when the extension applies.
  • Extension Definition: define the new attributes or elements with UML diagrams, attribute descriptions, and child-element descriptions.
  • Security Considerations: discuss any security implications of the extension and how users should deploy it securely.
  • IANA Considerations: specify any registry entries or namespace registrations required; if none, say so explicitly.
  • Manageability Considerations: address operational and management aspects if relevant.
  • Appendices: XML Schema Definition for the extension, and example IODEF Documents using the extension.

Following this structure ensures reviewers know what to expect and extensions are documented consistently.
sections.eli5: Here's the outline to use when proposing a new box: what's the problem, define terms, when is it useful, what does the new box look like, is it secure, does IANA need to know, anything else an operator should care about, plus examples.

children.note: Add new values to existing fields (Incident@purpose, Contact@role, etc.)
